ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Drug research in India 
*221. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY. Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps his Ministry is taking or propose to take to focus on drug 
research in India; 
(b) the money spent on drug research during the last five years, year-wise; 
(c) the money spent on drug research, percentage-wise, out of profit earned 
by companies during the last five years, year-wise; and 
(d) the measures Government are taking to make India a leader in drug 
development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPILSIBAL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Ministry of Science and Technology is taking several steps and 
measures to focus on drug research  to make India a leader in drug 
development. Some of these steps and measures are: 
increasing the outlay for Research and Development (R&D) on drug 
research

introducing newer programmes for drugs and pharmaceuticals R&D' 
encouraging collaborative R&D projects among laboratories/ 
institutions/industry in modern and Indian Systems of Medicine i.e. 
public-private partnership 
establishing state-of-the-art facilities 
strengthening the human resource development through research 
fellowships, young scientist scheme, etc. 
establishment of Pham iaceutical Research a nd Development Support 
fund(PRDSF) 
the Technology Development Boar(i of DST is supporting research and 
commercialization in the private sector, with, good results, and 
organising Pharma Industry-Institutional interactive meet, seminar, 
symposia on modern, ayurveda, unani, siddha systems of medicine 
including veterinary drug development. 
(b) During the last five years Ministry of Science and Technology has spent 
Rs.5143 lakhs in 1999-2000, Rs.4187 lakhs in 2000-01, Rs. 4948 lakhs in 
2001-02, R8.6340 lakhs in 2002-03 and Rs. 8910 lakhs in 2003-04 respectively 
on drug research. 
(c) No such data is collected. 
(d) As provided in part (a) of the question above.

SHRIRAMAMUNIREDDY SfRIGIREDDY The average research and 
development spending on pharma companies in India is less than two per cent of 
their turnover. The Minister has also referred to the Phamnaceutical Research and 
Development Support Fund with an initial corpus of Rs.2,297 cnores. I would like 
to know what action-plan the Ministry has prepared to optimally utilise this 
Fund on drug research in India. 
 
 
2

[16 December, 2004] RAJYASABHA 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: First of all, Mr. Chairman, Sir, as far as the 
Pharmaceutical Research and Development Support Fund is concerned, we were 
hoping that we would get a corpus of Rs.150 crores, but, unfortunately, that 
was not forthcoming. Originally, we r eceived only Rs.25 crores. We were 
supposed to spend on our R&D from the interest earned out of Rs.25 crores. Now, 
of course, we have the corpus of Rs. 150 crores but that is not enough. We need 
much more money for R&D, especially in the area of developing new drugs. So, 
we are hoping, and we are, in fact, persuading the Finance Ministry to allocate 
more funds to us. We have also moved to the Planning Commission for that. 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDYSIRIGIREDDY: Sir, my next supplementary 
is based on the reply that the hon. Minister has just now given, a corpus 
fund of Rs.150 crores, and all that. The recent collaborations by major 
pharmaceutical companies, particular ly the companies which are now 
having collaboration with the public sector and also with other big private 
companies, with international giants is a good sign for giving a right direction 
to drug research in India. In view of this, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister what kind of technical, scie ntific or collaborative assistance is 
extended by the Government of India to companies in the private sector 
during the last three years.  
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL; Mr Chairman, Sir, as far as we are concerned, we have 
several avenues of collaboration with private industry. We are devising a new 
scheme for the purposes of collaboration because we have come to the conclusion 
that it is impossible for a private company alone to develop drugs, especially in the 
social development Sector Who is going to develop a drug for T.B.? The big MNCs 
in the world am not going to develop a drug forTB., HIV&AIDSand malaria. For 
all these, drugs have to be developed by us and by the less developed world. We 
believe this cannot be done without public-private partnerships. And we are 
moving in that direction. In fact, we have recently discovered, after 40 years a 
new molecule for tuberculosis called DUPOTERB, result of an indigenous 
collaboration, and that also is a public-private partnership. We are asking 
private companies to come to us. If we find that the project is viable, we give a 
loan. We, sometimes, give 70 per cent of the amount required. But, of course, 
that is going to be returned to us as we change a very low rate of interest, i.e. 
about three per cent. We are fast moving forward in this 
 
3

RAJYA SABHA (16 December, 2004] 
direction through public-private partnerships for the purposes of developing new 
drugs. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I am somewhat surprised that the 
ICMR which is supposed to be the basic organisation for research is not even 
mentioned here. These areas usually used to be under the health Ministry. Could 
the hon. Minister kindly let me know (a) whether there is a close collaboration 
with the ICMR, which is not mentioned in the answer? (b) What is the progress 
in two particular areas? One is the combined drugs against HIV/AIDs, and the 
second is the population control; the anti-pregnancy vaccines, the male pills. 
There were a lot of very encouraging leads 30 years ago. They all seem to have 
petered out. What is the progress on that? 
..SHRIKAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chainnan, Sir, basically, the ICMR is not under my 
Ministry. But I will be more than happy to answer the question that my friend put 
to me. One of the things that I have done is, in fact to tell the ICMR that in 
many of the areas, the R&D that we work on should be done together, because the 
Department of Biotechnology worKs in some areas and the ICMR works in other 
areas. I called the Secretaries together and asked them to collaborate their efforts. 
Now, in the context of the question of HIV and AIDS, thatisexactly what! have 
done. I asked the Department of Biotechnology to find out the best candidates 
available so that these two Departments can work together instead of working 
separately on the same drugs. Let us find out the best candidates available and 
then invest in ihem. As far as anti-pregnancy and the male pill is concerned, 
again, that is not part of my Ministry. If the hon. Member wants, 1 will find out 
from the ICMR and give him the appropriate reply. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Sir, the hon. Minister would certainly 
appreciate that the pharma companies in this country are mostly private 
companies, including multi-national companies. I am just putting the 
question. To my knowledge, they hardly spend anything on research and 
development. Would the Minister be kind enough to explain the percentage of the 
total turnover of the pharma market that has been spent on research and

you have rightly referred?

[16 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, as far as tiie percentage of investment on 
R&D qua net sales turnover is concerned, let me tell you, that foreign entities, that is, 
multinationals, R&D concerned, the percentage ranges anywhere between 8 per cent and 
20 per cent, which is a huge amount. Briefly stated, f^flr. Chairman, Sir, the pharma sector 
has 25,000 companies. Of the 25,000 companies, 15,000 companies are in the samll-scale 
sector. Five thousand companies are bulk drug companies. So, you are really left with 5,000 
companies which are biggish companies. As far as they are concemed, their expenditure on 
R&D ranges anywhere between 3 per cent and 5 per cent. Some of our phamna companies, and, in 
particular, Shanta Biotech, have an R&D expenditure of 27.4 per cent this year. Some of 
our private pharma companies are doing exceptionally well and investing more and more in 
R&D. What I am really concerned about, and this is something which I would like to 
inform the House, is that, if you look at the researchers in R&D per m illion of 
population, we don't have enough human resources. 1 will give you some figures which will, 
perhaps, astound the House. In a country like Britain, it is 1.9 per cent of R and D per 
million; in Germany, it is 2.5 per cent; in Finland, it is 3.4 per cent; in US, it is 2.8 per 
cent; in Brazil, it is 1.1 per cent; India comes at the bottom of the list with 0.7 per 
cent. In this country, the problem really is that we have not got enough human resources, 
manpower, and unless we put more and more money into education and in education 
science, we are not going to bring that figure up and our R and D output is going to be 
minimal. So, we need more investment in human resources. 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD. Sir, in the Minister reply we also see a mention 
about collaborative R and D projects in modern and Indian System of Medicines. I am 
sure, you would be aware of the recent reports, particularly, in the USA, complaining inter 
alia that Indian System of Medicines, have a lot of lethal metal contents, mercury, etc. 
They are also reported in the newspapers today. What worries me is that these reports are 
directly proportionate, in a way, to the increasing acceptability of Indian System of Medicines 
like Ayurveda in Europe and the US. My questions to you are: (a) Is your Ministry 
taking any step to dispel this kind of misinformation? (b) Do you also propose to 
make any international campaign in the light of the scientific viability of the Indian 
System of Medicines?

RAJYASABHA [16 December, 2004] 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL; Sir, in fact ,we are laying great emphasis on the 
Indian System of Medicines and traditional medicines.As far as these reports 
are concerned, many of these reports are motivated. My Ministry in 
collaboration with the Ministry of Health will take effective steps to ensure the 
desire of such misinformation is not perpetrated. 
DR. VIJAYMALLYA; Sir, India has an extremely attractive environment 
with the necessary human resources to encourage huge investment in basic 
research and development in the pharmace utical sector Recently, one of the 
word's foremost multinational companies actually consciously located their 
Research and Devevlopment Wing in Singaproe. And, the reason cited was 
that there were not enough Intellectual Property Protection Rights in India. I 
would like the Minister to kindly note, being myself the Chairman of 
theAventis Pharma Limited, a multinational drug company, that there is a 
reluctance to invest in India because of lack of patent protection. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Mr Chairman, Sir, again, this does not involve my 
Minsitry. But I will be more than happy to answer this question. First of all, the 
Third Amendment Bill, the latest amendment, would ensure that our patents 
are in conformity with international obligations. The Government will be 
taking a position very soon in that regard, say, by January, 2005. As far as the 
investment climate is concerned, which my learned friend is talking about, in 
fact, it is fast changing. Multinationals have been coming to me and evincing 
extreme interest in investing in India. More and more multinationals are 
investing in India. Presently some multinationals are collaborating with 
Indian pharmaceutical companies by transferring their know-how and 
technology to them for the purpose of manufacture of products for the simple 
reason that we have great human talent, and we are a low cost economy 
Nobody else in the world has this combination available. So, India is going to 
forge ahead in this regard. We are going to be the leaders in the pharmaceutical 
industry in the years to come, and we are ready to compete with anybody else 
in the world.

SHRI DWfJENDRANATH SHARMAH: Sir, in my question, I wanted to 
know how many districts were going to be connected by cellular phone 
services. The Minister has given details pertaining to District Headquarters. Sir, a 
major drawback in the development of the North-Eastern Region is 
communication, and there are a lot of interior places, hilly places, in the North-
East which are not connected by cellular phone services. May I know from the 
hon. Minister whether the Government has taken any steps for extending such 
cellular phone services to interior places? 
SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN: Sir, the hon. Member is right. Deployment of 
cellular phone services in the North-Eastern area is slow compared to the rest of 
the parts of the country. The reason is that we had awarded licenses to BSNL 
only in the end of March 03, and the wori< started mainly in the beginning of this 
year. Only 16 districts are left to be covered, and we are sure that we will be able 
to cover them by August of next year.

Apart from BSNL services, there are some private players of cellular phone, 
particulariy Reliance Mobile Services, which are there in the North-East in one or 
two places. But the service of these private cellular phones is very bad, and there 
are a Iqt of complaints from the public. I would like

Facilities to Gramin Dak Sevaks 
*235. SHRl C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether three lakh Gramin Dak Sevaks maintaining communications 
services to rural Indian are being deni ed all facilities and benefits despite 
Supreme Court's ruling to treat them as holders of civilian posts; 
(b) the details of their pending demands; and 
(c) the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRl DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) The Hon'ble Supreme 
Court, in the case of RK. Rajamma, 1977 (3) SCC 1994, has held that 
although an Extra Departmental Ag ent (EDA), now called Gramin Dak 
Sevak (GDS) holds a civil post under the administrative control of the State, 
such a post is outside the regular Civil Services. The EDAs now 
43 

RAJYASABHA [16 December, 2004] 
called Gramin Dak Sevaks, therefore, do  not form part of the regular Civil 
Services as they are not regular Government employees, but a class apart. They are 
part-time employees employed for a period upto a maximum of 5 hours per day 
Consequent upon the recommendations of the Justice Talwar Committee, the 
issue of grant of status of regular Govt, employees to the Gramin Dak Sevaks was 
examined by the Group of Ministers (GoM) and thereafter by the Government in 
1998, but not accepted. Subsequently while examining the issue of change of 
nomenclature of the Extra Departmental Agents, the matter was again 
considered by the Group of Ministers and thereafter by the Govemment in 
December, 2000 but rejected. As such Gramin Dak Sevaks are not eligible for all 
benefits and facilities which are admissible to the regular Government 
employees. Their terms and conditions of employment are governed by a 
separate set of rules called Gramin Dak Sevaks Conduct & Employment 
Rules, 2001. 
(b) The Gramin Dak Sevaks have been making demands, the major ones 
being grant of status, for grant of pension (Social Security), maternity leave for 
women GDSs, all trade union facilities for the office bearers of their union & 
merger of 50% Dearness Allowance w ith the Time Related Continuity 
Allowance. 
(c) The reaction of the Govt, on the above issues is as below: 
Demand for grant of pension/social security: While examining the 
recommendations of Justice Talw ar Committee set up in 1985, the 
Government did not find the demand for grant of pension feasible. However, a new 
element viz. SeveranceAmountof Rs. 20,000/-or 30,000/-depending on the period 
of employment has been introduced w.e.f. 17.12.1998. 
Demand for grant of maternity leave: The recommendation of the Justice 
Talwar Committee for grant of leave including maternity leave was considered by 
the Government. However, paid leave at the rate of 10 days for each half year 
without the facility of carry forward or encashment was accepted. Further 
Gramin Dak Sevaks can avail leave without allowances upto maximum of 180 
days in a year. 
Demand for grant of all trade union facilities: The All India Postal Extra 
Departmental Employees Union has already been availing of a number of trade union 
facilities. However, their demand forgrantof facility of Foreign Service and Special 
Casual Leave was considered by the Government, but not accepted due to the 
reasons that these are available only to  the Associations/Unions of regular 
Government servants. 
44 

[16 December, 2004] RAJYASABHA 
Demand for Merger of 50% Dearne ss Allowance (DA) with Time 
Related Continuity Allowance (TRCA) of Gramin Dak Sevaks: The 
Government had allowed Time Related Continuity Allowance (TRCA) of 
Gramin Dak Sevaks: as full and final se ttlement of Justice Talwar Committee 
recommendations and Cabinet had approved merger of DA only for regular Central 
Government employees. Therefore, the benefit of merger of 50% DA with 
TRCA has not been extended to the GDSs who are outside the regular Civil

Norms for Opening Post Offices 
1. Norms for opening Extra Departmental Branch Post Offices:

respect of parent'post office does not increase beyond the permissible limit nor is its 
income reduced below the minimum prescribed.

Demand for Scrapping the Restructured Pension Scheme 
1561. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of LABOUR' AND 
EMF'LOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it Is a fact that the restructured pension scheme being monitored by the 
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority of India has come into effect 
from 1st January, 2004; 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme; 
(c) whether there is demand for scrapping the scheme and reverting back to the old 
scheme from certain quarters; and 
(d) if sc. Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K CHANDRA SEKHAR 
RAO): (a) to (d) A new restructured defined contribution pension system is mandatory for all 
new Central Government recruits (excluding Armed Forces, in the first stage) with effect 
from 1st January, 2004. The monthly contribution is 10 percent of the salary and Dearness 
Allowance to be paid by the employee and matched by the Central Government. The New 
Pension System (NPS) will be available, on a voluntary basis, to all persons including 
self employed professionals and others in the unorganised sector However, mandatory 
programmes under the Employees' Provident Fund Organization (EPFO) and other special 
provident funds continue to operate as per the existing system under the Employees' 
Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 and other special Acts governing 
these funds. Workers in the organized sector would continue to be governed by schemes 
under these Acts. 
After extensive consultations and taking into account the views of various Sections, in 
order to promote old age income security and to fix Government's pension liability up 
front. Government have decided to have a funded pension scheme where members have 
investment choices.

with respect to Small scale industries; and 
(b) if so, what strategy has since been evolved to achieve this objective? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHAVIR PRASAD): 
(a) and (b) The Government has always been conscious of the need to end "Inspector Raj" in 
the context of the small scale industries (SSI) sector. Accordingly, ail State 
Governments and Union Territory Administrations have been advised to look into the 
returns submitted under various existing labour laws by small scale industries as self 
certified and treat them as prima-facie compliance. In addition, a 'Small Enterprises 
Development Bill' is under consideration of the Government, which will inter alia, seek 
to address the issue of reducing and streamlining the inspection of SSI units under 
various laws, at present applicable to them.

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION OF THE CHAIR 
Re:   Reported statement by Shri K. Natwar Singh (Minister of iExternal Affairs) 
In Seoul on Nuclear Policy of the Government of India 
THE HEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Si", to 
benefit from the hon. Prime Ministers presence in the House, I wani to seek certain vital 
clarifications covering country's, firstly, nuclear policv, and secondly, very important aspect of 
continuity of policy regarding national security. If I might submit, Sir, with due regard the 
question of r<3sponsibility of the entire Cabinet in regard to statements made or not made 
and also the resultant uncertainty that is created about the foreign pcilicy, I wish to draw the 
attention to certain reports that have appeared. Sir, I am ready to accept that simply based 
on the reports we cannot structure an opinion. Therefore, I sought further details of these 
reports. 7776 Indran Express was carrying the report, and then I accessed the PTI. Thereafter I 
also accessed the report from Seoul because this report was attributed to the hon. the 
Minister of External Affairs, who among other things, has said that India's previous Government 
was responsible for the decision to enter the nuclear stand-off with Pakistan. This I cite. 
Sir, because this is given in quote. Thereafter, he directly or indirectly expresses a 
certain regret saying, "But regret would be futile". I am concerned because this portion 
of the statement of the hon. the Minister of External Affairs, of course, is questioning the 
established policy of the Government, not simply of the Government to which I had the 
honour to belong, but also of the present Government, and naturally it creates an 
uncertainty about where does the present Government stand on this vital aspect. May I 
submit also, Sir, that it falsefies the achievements of the country because the Apsara, 
experimental reactor established in 1956, and the entire nuclear programme of the 
country cannot be just one Govemmenfj! programme. I have said so repeatedly in the House. 
Whatever be the nuclear achievement, the policy of the Government is really a 
continuit/ from the Nehru-Bhabha days' Apsara to the days of late 
234 

[16 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Mrs. Gandhi and all subsequent Prime Ministers including late Shri Rajiv Gandhi, Shri 
Narsimha Rao and others. Therefore, to suggest that it is the previous Government is 
regrettable. What he also does regrettably, is to take the contentions of our domestic politics 
to foreign shores and to give voice to the domestic politics. The Minister for External Affairs 
is entirely within his rights to find fault with the previous Government and to criticise us to his 
heart's content, which, I think, he is quite given to doing. But, if he were to do so on shores 
other than India, then, it is really breaking a tradition which successive generations of 
political leaders have followed. Also this suggestion, Sir, as he has done that the previous 
Government entered into a nuclear stand-off with neighbouring Pakistan, in fact belittles the 
totality of the country's nuclear programme. We have repeatedly said, I have said so in the 
House, that India's nuclear programme is not Pak-centric. It was never intended to be 
Pak-centric. It is not focussed on Pakistan and it is a much wider concern that has 
persuaded India in its quest for having a nuclear parity with the rest of the world. Therefore, 
to belittle India, India's achievements and to reduce it as stand-off, I think, is a great 
disservice to India. I am very glad that the hon. Prime Minister is here and, that is why, I have 
suggested and I would request the hon. Prime Minister to clarify because we cannot simply 
wait for the hon. the Minister of External Affairs to return and further clarify what he said. These 
are the reports that have appeared. I have tried to access the reports in every sense 
possible, whether in Seoul or PTI or Indian Express and it is also. Sir, that so far as country's 
security and nuclear policy goes, the Prime Minister's role is pre-eminent. It would, therefore, 
not be suffice for anybody to suggest that until the hon. Minister is back, we should wait 
and only then seek a clarification to end the uncertainty about security; also for Cabinet 
responsibility because the Prime Minister is Prime Minister and nobody else can be the 
Prime Minister and claim to make policy on behalf of the Prime Minister At least, that is the 
theory on which we work. I would, therefore, urge the Prime Minister to immediately clarify 
all these various things that have arisen on account of the reports appearing and the direct 
statement, that I have quoted, made by the hon. the Minister of External Affairs. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal); Sir, before the Prime Minister's response to this, 
since this is a very serious issue which has been brought 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2004] 
to the at1;ention of the House by the hon. Leader of the Opposition, for whom I have the 
greatest regard, will the hon. Prime Minister also clarify certain other points, which actually 
arise out of the issue which he has articulatesd? Now, hon. Leader of the Opposition has 
maintained that the previous Government had really tried to consolidate the consensus that 
was there in the country on foreign policy issues, especially our nuclear policy. Now this 
House has been witness to furious debates on the question of nuclear policy in the 
aftermath of 12th of May, 1998, when the Government in which the hon. Leader of the 
Opposition was also a member, went for nuclear detonation in Pokhran. Subsequent to that, 
all Indian newspapers published a letter written by the then hon. Prime Minister, Shri Atal 
Behari Vajpayee, to President George W. Bush that this is the response to our 
security....C/nferrupf/onsJ. Yes, I mean, Mr. Bill Clinton. We are so enamoured by George 
W. Bush that sometimes, we also get confused as if that was the past, present and future of 
the United States. Now, that lelter specifically mentioned that the immediate provocation or 
inspiration fc r Pokhran II was our security concern over Pakistan and China, and, which, ! 
believe also created a lot of diplomatic discomfort for the Indian Government at that 
point of time. 
Subsequently, when we had debate on that issue in this House as well as the other 
House, I think there was a great divide across the Indian polity as to whether what was 
done by the Government of Atal Behari Vajpayeeji represented a national consensus. 
And, Sir, all of us, a large body of political parties in fact maintained that what was done 
by that Government at that point of time was a major break in the tradition of the foreign 
policy making of this country in the sense that there was no national consensus, and, it was 
contrary to the electoral commitment given by the NDA in its common election 
manifesto.

position of the Government, but we would also like to be clarified on the question whether 
really there was a continuity of national consensus in terms of foreign policy making, and, 
specially, the nuclear policy.
